title: Koymans–Pagano Stevenhagen conjecture (negative Pell) — '−1 as a target' analogy
connection: Koymans–Pagano proved Stevenhagen's conjecture on the density of D for which x² − Dy² = −1 is solvable; negative Pell asks whether −1 is a norm of a unit, ES's B2 asks whether −1 lies in the divisor quotient set.
why: Both are '−1 hitting' problems whose obstructions are 2-adic/Rédei; the negative-Pell proof technology handles exactly the −1 target.
first_step: Write the e-slice event for e prime as 'class of −1 in a ray class group generated by primes dividing N' and compare with the negative-Pell 4-rank/8-rank framework.

title: Weight-1 Eisenstein coefficients: ES class-divisor counts as Eisenstein Fourier coefficients along an AP
connection: #{d | N : d ≡ −1 (mod m)} = φ(m)^{−1} Σ_χ χ̄(−1) Σ_{d|N} χ(d), and Σ_{d|N} χ(d) are Fourier coefficients of Eisenstein series (weight 1 for odd χ); ES Type I at fixed p sums these at N = 4Cp+1 along C.
why: Turns ES into sums of automorphic Fourier coefficients along arithmetic progressions — a setting with spectral (shifted-convolution) technology and exact main terms.
first_step: Write R(p) explicitly as Σ_C Σ_{χ mod 4C} χ̄(−1) a_{E_χ}(4Cp+1) and separate the χ = principal/real contributions to see the main term and the T1-relevant piece.
refs: Diamond–Shurman, A First Course in Modular Forms (2005), ch. 4

title: Nelson / Michel–Venkatesh subconvexity for Type I class-group twisted sums
connection: Subconvexity for GL₂ twists by class-group characters (Michel–Venkatesh) gives equidistribution of Heegner/CM objects; Type I class-group sums at discriminant −16d are such twisted sums.
why: Michel–Venkatesh-type bounds are what Duke-type equidistribution at a single discriminant needs.
first_step: Write the Type I count at fixed (p,d) as Σ_{ψ ∈ Ĉl(−16d)} ψ(stuff)·L-values and identify which subconvexity bound would give positivity.
refs: Michel–Venkatesh, The subconvexity problem for GL2, Publ. IHES 111 (2010)
Nelson, Bounds for standard L-functions, arXiv:2109.15230

title: Baker's linear forms in logarithms: bounds for exceptional structured solutions
connection: Baker/Matveev bound linear forms in logs; ES solutions with denominators in multiplicatively structured families (powers, S-units) lead to exponential Diophantine equations.
why: Gives explicit bounds for the S-unit/smooth barrier items, making them computational.
first_step: Write the ES equation with x,y,z restricted to ⟨2,3,5,7⟩ and solve completely via Baker + LLL reduction.
refs: Matveev, An explicit lower bound for a homogeneous rational linear form in logarithms, Izv. Math. 64 (2000)

title: Chain basis ⇔ representation of the binary lattice [[v,−1],[−1,t]] with a prescribed orthogonal vector
connection: A chain basis exists iff the ternary lattice L contains a primitive binary sublattice ≅ [[v,−1],[−1,t]] whose orthogonal complement direction meets L appropriately. This is a 'representation of binary forms by ternary forms' problem with an extra condition.
why: Representation of binary forms by ternary/quaternary forms has deep equidistribution results (Ellenberg–Venkatesh; Einsiedler–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh). These give existence for large discriminant, but with growing discriminant here.
first_step: Formulate: for each binary form b of disc ≈ 4tv−4 ≤ X, is b represented by a ternary of det p in the non-square genus with the extra e₃ condition? Compare with the Ellenberg–Venkatesh hypotheses.
refs: Ellenberg–Venkatesh, Local-global principles for representations of quadratic forms (Invent. 2008)

title: Siegel–Weil formula for the certificate genus: average over the genus is the BM main term
connection: Siegel–Weil: the genus-averaged representation number is a product of local densities, i.e. an Eisenstein coefficient. BM's main term is exactly such a product. The difference from a single class is a cusp-form coefficient.
why: In the quadratic-form toolbox, pointwise lower bounds come from 'Eisenstein main term ≫ cusp error'. ES's analogue has main term log²p, too small for cusp bounds; this is the native statement of the B3 obstacle.
first_step: Compute the ratio of BM main term to the trivial cusp-form bound in the best available quadratic encoding (rank 4, QUATERNION_ES); record the exponent gap.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0181] Express M_BM as Π of local densities (singular series) for the (★) variety and compare with the BL Brauer-corrected Siegel–Weil heuristics; look for the 'classes' whose average it is.

title: Eisenstein–Kronecker / Lerch: word counts as special values of partial zeta functions
connection: Sums over divisors in residue classes are partial zeta values of ℚ at s = 0 for ray classes. Per-p word counts are finite combinations of such divisor sums, possibly expressible via partial zeta values of real quadratic fields (via γ_w).
why: Partial zeta values at s = 0 are rational and given by Shintani/Siegel formulas, which could turn the sign sum into a finite computable rational expression with integrality.
first_step: Attempt: express Σ_{words} (A/p) at prime p as Σ of ζ(0, 𝔞) over narrow ideal classes of Q(√D) for D from traces; check numerically for small p.
refs: Shintani 1976 (values of zeta at non-positive integers)

title: Class-number formula positivity for the BM correction T(p)
connection: Dirichlet's real-character case: L(1,χ) = (const)·h > 0 because h is a positive integer. M_BM = M₀ − T(p) with T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB); express T(p) through L(1, (·/p)·ψ) for small auxiliary ψ, i.e. through class numbers of Q(√±p m).
why: If T(p) ≈ c·L(1,(·/p))·(log p) + …, then integrality/positivity of class numbers and known upper bounds of L(1,χ) give an exact grip on the main term, beyond Burgess.
first_step: Inspect BM_CORRECTED_COUNT / BOARD2_SLATE main-term formulas for p-dependent L-value factors; if present, apply Siegel/Burgess lower bounds.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0051] Write T(p) as a Dirichlet series in (·/p) with multiplicative weights; extract the main term as a combination of L(1,(·/p)χ) and check numerically against computed T(p).

title: Efficient congruencing in the level variable
connection: Wooley's method lifts solutions p-adically and compares congruence classes at several scales. ES solutions as solutions of p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) for growing 4uB: congruencing across scales of the modulus.
why: Odd but not empty: ES is literally a family of congruences whose modulus is a variable; congruencing-type iteration handles such 'modulus as variable' counts in VMVT.
first_step: Write the count of (u,B) with 4uB ≤ Q and p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB as a mean value of a Weyl-like sum and see if the efficient-congruencing recursion has an analogue.

title: Index argument: subgroup generated by prime factors of N in (ℤ/4C)*
connection: Artin-type proofs control the index of ⟨a⟩ in F_p*. ES level C fails iff no subproduct of prime factors of N = 4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 (4C). If the factors generate a subgroup H ∌ −1, failure is automatic; if −1 ∈ H, failure needs few factors. Study the index of H as p varies.
why: Separates the 'algebraic' failure (−1 ∉ H) from the 'combinatorial' one (too few factors), which need different tools (characters vs. zero-sum theory).
first_step: For the hard primes and C ≤ 100, compute H = ⟨prime factors of 4Cp+1⟩ mod 4C and classify each failing level as algebraic or combinatorial.
refs: Heath-Brown, Q. J. Math. 37 (1986) 27-38 (Artin's conjecture for primitive roots)

title: Move to a nonabelian encoding where character ratios decay
connection: Ore/Waring for finite simple groups works because |χ(g)/χ(1)| is small for large groups (quasirandomness). ES's character expansion lives in abelian groups (ℤ/4uB)* where all ratios are 1 — no decay. Find a nonabelian group encoding (SL₂(ℤ/q), Heisenberg, quaternion units mod q) where the certificate count expands over characters with small ratios.
why: The abelian encoding may be the reason no pointwise cancellation is visible; nonabelian Fourier analysis has built-in square-root savings from representation dimensions.
first_step: Express the SL₂-form certificate condition modulo q as a class-function count in SL₂(ℤ/q) and expand via Frobenius' formula; estimate the non-trivial character contribution.
refs: Liebeck-O'Brien-Shalev-Tiep, The Ore conjecture, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 12 (2010) 939-1008

title: Trivial vs needed pointwise bound for the non-genus part X(p)
connection: Ramanujan/Deligne improved the trivial (Hecke) bound to the sharp one. For ES, compute the trivial pointwise bound for |X(p)| (from the character expansion) and the bound needed (|X| < M_gen); quantify the gap in powers of log p.
why: Measures how much 'Ramanujan-type' saving ES needs in the non-genus part.
first_step: Bound |X(p)| ≤ Σ_q Σ_{χ mod q, ord ≥ 3} |stuff|/φ(q) trivially and evaluate numerically against M_gen for test p.

title: Function-field Bombieri–Vinogradov at level beyond 1/2 (Sawin–Shusterman style)
connection: Sawin–Shusterman proved FF results (e.g. level of distribution beyond 1/2 for primes, twin-prime-type statements for large q) unavailable over Z. ES-type existence at a given P via primes in progressions could follow in FF.
why: If an FF ES-for-all-P proof needs exactly a level-θ > 1/2 distribution statement, that pins the integer analytic input needed (a Elliott–Halberstam-type hypothesis).
first_step: Check whether Sawin–Shusterman 'On the Chowla and twin primes conjectures over F_q[T]' gives distribution of P-tied polynomials in progressions to modulus degree > deg/2; map to Type I.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Huang–Vaughan exceptional set asymptotic for a/n = 1/x+1/y → model for ES exceptions in a single slice
connection: Huang–Vaughan prove E_a(N) ~ C(a) N (log log N)^{2^{m−1}−1}/(log N)^{1−1/2^m} for fixed a, via 'delicate analysis of the underlying group structure' ((Z/aZ)^* and subgroups). ES needs a union over slices a = 4x − n with x varying.
why: Their group-structure analysis is exactly the 'divisor in a class' combinatorics; joint control over many a would be a quantitative almost-all ES with structure.
first_step: Read Huang–Vaughan's method and identify whether it extends to 'for some a in a set A(n)' with A depending on n (union bound + correlation).

title: Hooley's Δ-function and concentration of divisors ↔ the lottery's 'ticket clumping'
connection: Hooley's Δ(n) = max_u #{d | n : u < d ≤ eu}. Divisors clumping in short ranges reduces the effective number of independent tickets in the ES lottery.
why: If Δ of the relevant p-tied integers is small on average, a second-moment argument gives almost-all ES with better exceptional bounds.
first_step: Check Hall–Tenenbaum results on Δ on average and adapt to the family {4Cp + 1 : C ≤ C₀}.

title: Huang–Vaughan mean value theorems for binary Egyptian fractions
connection: Mean values of the number of representations a/n = 1/x + 1/y over n (and a) are known with secondary terms. These are the 2-term building blocks of ES slices.
why: Combining 2-term mean values over a = 4x − p gives ES counts; correlations between different a are the missing ingredient for pointwise results.
first_step: Read arXiv:1108.0096 / 1109.2274 for the error terms; see if they allow a correlation estimate across a.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0081] Check the exact statements of Huang–Vaughan and whether their mean-value bound is uniform enough to sum over the ES parameter x.
refs: unverified: Huang, Vaughan, Mean value theorems for binary Egyptian fractions (J. Number Theory)

title: Chebotarev-in-short-ranges (Lagarias–Odlyzko, Thorner–Zaman) for certificate fields
connection: If ES certificates at p correspond to p splitting in one of a family of number fields K_C (C ≤ C₀), ES ⇔ every p splits in some K_C with C small. Effective Chebotarev bounds give least primes splitting, not 'every prime splits somewhere'.
why: Clarifies the logical shape: ES is a covering of all primes by Chebotarev sets — exactly the shape where only finite abelian coverings are classical (and Mordell blocks them).
first_step: Pointer: formulate ES as a Chebotarev covering problem and list the fields K_C for small C.

title: Free leading coefficients in FF: exceptional set is EXACTLY the squares once q > (n+1)² (one Weil sum)
connection: EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD §1.3: for the numerator-free U union (U'_q, not ES_q itself), without the sign normalization the exceptional set equals the squares for large q, proved by a Weil sum over q − 1 unit shifts. Over Z there are only two unit shifts (±1), so the step has no integer analogue.
why: Shows precisely what 'many units' buys: a character sum over units averages out the colour constraint. Over Z the replacement would be an average over a p-tied family of 'shifts' of size → ∞ with Weil-quality cancellation.
first_step: Identify an integer family of shifts (e.g. multipliers C ≤ C₀) whose character sum could replace the q − 1 unit shifts, and estimate its cancellation (Burgess-range).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sums of reciprocals of small integers modulo p (Bourgain–Garaev / Shparlinski type)
connection: Results show every residue mod p is a sum of a bounded number k of reciprocals 1/x_i (mod p) with x_i ≤ p^ε-type bounds (check exact statements). ES needs an exact integer identity, but the modular version with small x_i is a necessary 'shadow' and its methods (multilinear Kloosterman sums) are the analytic engine of Type II counts.
why: If the modular statement with 3 reciprocals and x_i in ES-relevant ranges is provable for all p, then ES reduces to lifting (a size/sign condition) — a sharp 'local-to-global' gap.
first_step: Look up Shparlinski's results on 'sums of reciprocals in residue rings' and their term count/size; formulate the ES-implied congruences and check which are automatically satisfiable.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0334] Check Bourgain–Garaev 'Sumsets of reciprocals in prime fields and multilinear Kloosterman sums' (Izvestiya 2014) for the 3-term statement and its box sizes.
[signature-0076] Check the Bourgain–Garaev 'sumsets of reciprocals' results and whether the ES equation mod 4Cp+1 reduces to such a sumset.
refs: unverified: Bourgain, Garaev, Sumsets of reciprocals in prime fields and multilinear Kloosterman sums (Izv. 2014)
Shparlinski, On a question of Erdős and Graham (check)

title: Transfer statement A (from F_q[T] density-zero theorem): 'GRH ⇒ #{p ≤ N : ¬ES(p)} ≤ N^{1−δ}'
connection: The FF proof (one-prime identity + RH for Dirichlet L-functions in F_q[T]) suggests the integer statement: under GRH, the ES exceptional set has a power saving. Even a conditional statement of this shape is apparently not in the literature.
why: A clean conditional theorem would be a genuine (if conditional) advance and would quantify what the FF RH step buys over Z.
first_step: Check Elsholtz–Tao and later literature for any GRH-conditional exceptional bound; then try to run the FF argument with GRH-quality Bombieri–Vinogradov over Z.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Catalog: Vaughan almost-all for m/n (exceptions ≪ N exp(−c(m) log^{2/3} N))
connection: Vaughan almost-all for m/n (exceptions ≪ N exp(−c(m) log^{2/3} N)) ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: log². Obstruction: none. Status: proved almost all; Pomerance–Weingartner: c(m) = c/φ(m)^{1/3} uniformly for m ≤ log² N. Mechanism: large sieve over many independent Type I/II congruence families.
why: The almost-all mechanism; uniformity in m is new and quantifies how the almost-all exponent degrades with m.
first_step: Read PW's uniform version; check whether its proof gives an explicit c for m = 4 and whether it can be pushed to short intervals around a prime.

title: Feature: averaging over targets
connection: Dividing-line feature 'averaging over targets'. ES LACKS (pointwise in p). To supply it one could: find a 'self-averaging' trick: express ES(p) as an average over an auxiliary family indexed by p's divisors of p-tied integers (amplification)
why: Almost-all results (Vaughan) are via averaging; pointwise ones need amplification or rigidity.
first_step: See AMPLIFY_EXCEPTION.md for prior attempts; list which amplifiers have not been tried.

title: Feature: dimension / number of variables
connection: Dividing-line feature 'dimension / number of variables'. ES 3 variables with a single equation: below circle-method range. To supply it one could: add dummy variables with constraints (e.g. parametrised Type I/II as varieties of higher dimension with 2 equations) to reach circle-method range
why: Hasse principle for integral points is provable for many-variable forms (Birch).
first_step: Write the Type I parametrisation (a,d,f,…) as an affine variety and compute its dimension/degree; check Birch-type criteria.

title: Transfer: Chen-type switching over the C-variable
connection: Sieve the linear sequence N_C = 4Cp + 1 (C ≤ X, p fixed) to make N_C a P₂ = q·r; then ES needs q ≡ −1 mod 4C, equivalently r ≡ −1 mod 4C. Switching principle: count pairs via the other factor.
why: Fixed p, varying C: a one-dimensional linear sieve with level of distribution from Bombieri–Vinogradov-type results for the modulus-varying class condition.
first_step: Write the bilinear form Σ_{C} Σ_{qr = 4Cp+1} 1[q ≡ −1 (4C)] and check which equidistribution input (in q over moduli 4C) is needed.

title: Dirichlet-steering constructions: use primes in APs to steer a certificate
connection: Bounded-generation proofs choose an auxiliary prime q in an AP to make entries coprime/divisible as needed. For ES, choose a prime q ≡ 3 mod 4 dividing a p-tied integer (Obláth: q | p + 1) — steering requires q to divide something specific, not just lie in an AP.
why: Clarifies the gap: steering works when the auxiliary object is free (any prime in an AP), not when it must divide a fixed integer.
first_step: List ES certificate constructions where the auxiliary prime can be chosen freely in an AP (if any exist, they would prove ES).

title: Lower bounds for exceptional sets: can one prove ES's exceptional set (if nonempty) is infinite?
connection: For p + 2^k, failures come in APs (infinite). For ES, scaling preserves solvability only downward; an ES counterexample p need not imply others. Ask: does one failing prime force infinitely many failing integers (yes: none — ES(kp) can hold via other factors)?
why: Structure of potential exceptional sets clarifies disproof shapes (single sporadic vs infinite families).
first_step: Prove/disprove: if ES fails at prime p then it fails at p^k (probably false/irrelevant since 4/p^k = (1/p^{k-1})·4/p … check directions).

title: U(p) vs least QNR: ρ = −0.66
connection: Residual of U(p) correlates −0.66 with the least quadratic non-residue of p and +0.46 with #QNR among primes ≤ 29.
why: Least-QNR is Burgess/Vinogradov territory; a proof that U(p) ≥ 1 using 'some small prime is a QNR' (Linnik–Vinogradov n₂(p) ≪ p^{1/(4√e)+ε}) is exactly the Type-I mechanism.
first_step: Write the Type-I count as a sum over QNRs and check numerically that its main term scales with #QNR ≤ log p.

title: ESC zero set: non-squares are 105, 288, 336, 672, 1380, 29568, 41220, 57696, 97440, 255360, …, 2 402 400
connection: n with no word having a coordinate in 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − n): only 105 among odd non-squares ≤ 3·10⁶; the even ones are highly smooth (2402400 = 2⁵·3·5²·7·11·13).
why: The even zeros are irrelevant for ES but are a clean 'smooth-number obstruction' fingerprint of the same word equation.
first_step: Check whether even ESC zeros are exactly the n with n+1 and 2n+1 having no divisors in the required classes (characterise).

title: Share families as proof targets: squarefree / lcm-closed / no-3 sub-ES
connection: Sub-families that are a stable fraction of all solutions (shares 0.15, 0.377, 0.346) have ≤ 3 exceptions ≤ 10⁵, with exceptions among the ES-hardest primes.
why: If a sub-family is a stable share, any lower bound for U(p) transfers with a constant loss only if equidistribution of solutions in the sub-family condition holds pointwise — a precise 'equidistribution' lemma to aim for.
first_step: Test pointwise stability of the share: min over p ∈ [X, 2X] of share(p) vs mean share; if bounded below away from 0, record as conjecture.

title: Hyperbola decomposition of certificates
connection: Split divisor searches at the square root and treat small divisors and small complementary factors separately.
why: This avoids assuming every successful certificate lies in one convenient size range.
first_step: Derive a nonoverlapping hyperbola decomposition for one explicit certificate count.

title: Character orthogonality for the target class
connection: Express the target residue indicator using Dirichlet characters when the divisor is coprime to the modulus.
why: An exact character expansion separates the principal contribution from signed fluctuations.
first_step: Expand the divisor-class count for modulus 12 and compare numerically with direct enumeration.

title: A large-sieve formulation
connection: Ask whether the family of changing moduli and p-tied integers can be organized into a large-sieve-shaped quadratic form.
why: A shared quadratic form could control many residue searches simultaneously.
first_step: Write the exact matrix of character evaluations for bounded C and p, then check which large sieve formulations match it.

title: Dispersion between certificate families
connection: Compare cross-correlations of counts from two distinct auxiliary-parameter ranges rather than their separate means.
why: Mixed counts can measure whether two families fail together.
first_step: Derive the two-family second-moment expansion and isolate its diagonal terms.

title: Bilinear factor ranges
connection: Group auxiliary factorizations into dyadic boxes and inspect whether a bilinear sum emerges.
why: Bilinear structure gives more options than treating each divisor independently.
first_step: For one certificate equation, write the sum over two factor variables restricted to dyadic intervals.

title: Kloosterman-shaped inverse sums
connection: Look for modular inverses after solving the factor congruence for one variable and compare the resulting sums with Kloosterman-type phases.
why: Inverse phases are a concrete analytic structure, although a useful bound must be checked.
first_step: Derive the additive-character expansion for one factor congruence and identify its phase exactly.

title: Short character-sum templates
connection: Check whether short character-sum estimates can force one useful parameter value within a moving interval.
why: This is relevant only after a certificate condition has been reduced to a character pattern.
first_step: Derive a concrete character-pattern sufficient condition, then check whether Burgess-type estimates apply to its interval and polynomial.

title: Transference from a model problem
connection: Design a finite-field or random-factor analogue where a three-term certificate statement is tractable, then identify exactly what transfers.
why: A model can isolate the deterministic ingredient missing from a heuristic.
first_step: Prove a small finite-group subset-product statement and list which hypotheses actual auxiliary factors satisfy.

title: Specialization with integrality audits
connection: Investigate when a polynomial or rational-function identity remains an integral positive certificate after substituting an integer.
why: An identity specializes automatically where defined, but integrality and positivity require separate hypotheses.
first_step: Take one symbolic identity and derive all denominator divisibility and sign conditions after T→m.

title: Circle-method toy models with three terms
connection: Build a smoothed, bounded model of the three-denominator equation and explicitly separate the exact count from its analytic approximation.
why: A toy model can reveal which variable ranges supply enough averaging without claiming the full method works.
first_step: Write the orthogonality integral for a bounded integer version of the cleared equation and inspect its diagonal and singular contributions.

title: Delta-symbol decompositions of the residual
connection: Check whether an exact delta expansion can separate multiplicative variables in the cleared ES equation.
why: Separation could expose new bilinear structures, but convergence and range conditions must be verified.
first_step: Write the finite integer residual and compare exact delta-symbol formulas with its size and variable ranges.

title: Sum-of-squares (Positivstellensatz) certificate that the ES count is positive for a symbolic p in a residue class
connection: Positivstellensatz gives algebraic certificates of positivity of polynomials on semialgebraic sets; the ES count isn't polynomial in p, but a surrogate (e.g. a weighted divisor sum with explicit character expansion) could be expressed via finite sums over residues of p mod M.
why: SOS has proved inequalities in combinatorics (flag algebras) that were beyond human reach; the challenge is finding a finite algebraic surrogate.
first_step: Fix M = 840; express Σ_{C ≤ K} Σ_{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)} 1 ≥ (Σ over C of a quadratic-character sum in p mod stuff) and see if any lower bound depends only on p mod M.

title: Ray class fields and the splitting of p in ℚ(√−d, ζ_{4cd}): ES certificates as Frobenius conditions
connection: The condition 'an ideal of norm f dividing (p + 2c√−d) has f ≡ −p (mod 4cd)' is a condition on Frobenius of f in a ray class field mod 4cd of ℚ(√−d). Chebotarev gives density; ES needs existence for one (c,d) at each p.
why: Chebotarev-type existence for one prime p (not density) is where effective Chebotarev + GRH gives 'a prime of norm ≤ (log disc)²' — Lagarias–Odlyzko. But here f is not required prime, and the field depends on (c,d), so a *family* of ray class fields indexed by (c,d) is probed at the single prime p. Family versions of Chebotarev (e.g. Kowalski's large sieve for Frobenius) give almost-all; pointwise is the open shape.
first_step: Write the exact Frobenius statement for the Type I condition; check in Sage for p = 1009 and small (c,d) that the ray class description matches the divisor form; then search 'Chebotarev for a fixed prime over a family of fields'.
refs: Kowalski, The large sieve and its applications

title: Erdős–Kac for the number of prime factors of 4Cp+1 across C at fixed p: 'enough factors' heuristics
connection: The subset-product set is large when ω(4Cp+1) is large; the distribution of ω over C ≤ X at fixed p is Erdős–Kac-like (normal with mean log log). Some C have ω ≥ 2 log log; for those the subset-product set likely covers (ℤ/4C)^×... except a subgroup obstruction.
why: Separates 'few factors' (bad luck) from 'wrong subgroup' (structural) failure types; the structural type is the one a proof must address.
first_step: Classify failures of (p, C) for p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 100 into: ω ≤ 1; subgroup generated by factors misses −1; subgroup contains −1 but subset-products miss. Tabulate.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0404] Prove (or find in literature) Turán–Kubilius for {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} counting prime factors q ≤ X^{1/2}; then state the strongest 'class' statement this gives (likely only for prime factors q with q ≡ −1 mod 4C, q ≤ X: the small-prime-certificate family).
[tools-0249] Compute the empirical ω-distribution of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10^5 at hard vs typical primes.
refs: Erdős–Kac, The Gaussian law of errors in the theory of additive number theoretic functions, Amer. J. Math. 62 (1940)

title: Analogy with the 'least prime quadratic non-residue' problem: existence of ONE prime with a prescribed Legendre symbol
connection: Vinogradov's least-QNR problem asks for a prime q ≤ p^ε with (q/p) = −1 — a pointwise statement about one prime, proved via Burgess bounds (unconditionally q ≪ p^{1/(4√e)+ε}). ES needs one prime factor of some 4Cp+1 with a prescribed residue mod 4C — same flavour: 'one object with a prescribed character value'.
why: Burgess's method is a genuine pointwise technique for character values; the campaign's barrier notes say gate G4 'needs Vinogradov's conjecture' — but perhaps a Burgess-strength version suffices for a *weaker* ES-adjacent statement (e.g. ES for p with an extra parameter).
first_step: Formulate: is there a C ≤ p^θ such that 4Cp+1 has a prime factor q ≡ −1 mod 4C? Heuristically trivial for large θ (many C), but a Burgess-type proof would need to control characters mod 4C over C — the modulus varies with C. Check whether a 'variable modulus Burgess' (e.g. Heath-Brown's large sieve for real characters) gives it.
refs: Heath-Brown, 'A mean value estimate for real character sums' (1995)

title: Heath-Brown's large sieve for real characters applied to the family {χ_{4C}} at the fixed point p
connection: Heath-Brown's quadratic large sieve bounds Σ_C |Σ_n a_n (n/4C)|² over square-free C; with a_n supported on n = 4Cp+1... hmm the inner sum depends on C. Alternative: fix p, sum over C of the character sum Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} χ(d) for χ mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1 — the M_BM main term.
why: The campaign's M_BM is a sum over C of twisted divisor sums; a large-sieve input over C would control the *error* in the mean value, i.e. R(p) ≈ M_BM(p) — exactly the needed lower tail but only on average over p. Document the exact loss.
first_step: Read FRONTIER §2's M_BM derivation; identify the error term; check whether Heath-Brown's bound applies with the roles of modulus and argument as they are.

title: Upper-bound sieve as a positive tool: 'not all of 4Cp+1 (C ≤ K) can be prime' is provable — can 'not all can avoid class −1 mod 4C' be?
connection: Brun's sieve proves that among 4Cp+1, C ≤ K (K ≈ (log p)^A), not all are prime (indeed at most O(K/log p) are). The ES failure condition per C is weaker than primality (products of primes in a −1-free subgroup), but still a 'sifted' condition; the sieve gives an upper bound on how many C can have 4Cp+1 with ALL prime factors in a given subgroup H_C ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× (a Landau-type sieve, density 1/√log for index-2 H).
why: Upper-bound sieves (unlike lower-bound) are robust and pointwise in p! If the upper bound on #{C ≤ K : all prime factors of 4Cp+1 in H_C} is < K, we get a C that wins — a genuinely pointwise argument. The catch: H_C varies with C and the sieve dimension is ~1/2 per C, giving bound ≈ K/√(log p)... times a constant; if the constant is < 1 we win! Must check: does a Selberg upper-bound sieve over the SHORT interval of C ≤ K with p ≈ huge give K · Π (1 − 1/2q) ≈ K/√log K, not K/√log p — since the sieving primes relevant up to K only. Then the bound is K/√log K < K, trivially fine — but it only bounds those C with no SMALL (≤ K) prime factor outside H; larger prime factors are unsifted. So the argument fails without input on large prime factors. Record precisely.
first_step: Write the sifted set precisely: F_C(p) = 'every prime factor q of 4Cp+1 satisfies q ∈ H_C' where H_C is the subgroup generated... (H_C depends on all factors, circular — fix H_C = a maximal −1-free subgroup instead, which for 4C = 4 is {1 mod 4}). Then bound #{C ≤ K: 4Cp+1 ∈ ℕ_{H}} via Selberg with sieve dimension 1/2 restricted to primes ≤ z; compute the numeric bound for p = 10¹⁸, K = 10⁶, z = 10⁶ and see how far it is from K.

title: Meta: run the board on the single question 'what structure must the exceptional set F_∞ have if nonempty?' (disproof-side reasoning)
connection: Instead of asking how to prove ES, ask the dual: suppose F_∞ ∩ primes ≠ ∅; derive necessary properties of such a prime (all 4c²dp+1 have factors in −1-free subgroups mod 4cd for all (c,d) ≤ K; Legendre profile; size). Then check whether those properties are self-contradictory for p large (a sieve upper bound on 'prime constellations' of unbounded length).
why: The 'unbounded constellation' angle (item in batch 3) may be the cleanest potential contradiction: no prime can have 4c²dp+1 'nearly prime in a subgroup sense' for ALL (c,d) ≤ K with K → ∞ unless the subgroup condition is 'cheap' — quantify.
first_step: Write the necessary conditions for p ∈ F_K formally; estimate via sieve the number of p ≤ X in F_K; see if the estimate goes to 0 faster than 1 for K ≈ log X (that's the heuristic) and whether any step is provable.

title: Analogy: Waring's problem G(k) — every large n is a sum of s k-th powers; the 'every n' is forced by the circle method's major arcs dominating. ES's 'major arc' is M_BM; its 'minor arcs' are uncontrolled — can a circle method over the (c,d)-torus be set up at all?
connection: Write the certificate count as ∫ Σ_{c,d,f} e(α(stuff)) dα: the Type II equation ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 is a single Diophantine equation in (f, f′, c, d) with p fixed — a 4-variable equation of degree 4 (f·f′ − 4c²d·p); the circle method needs many variables relative to degree, and here the number of variables is 4 and the 'size' is tied to p. Birch's condition fails spectacularly. Quantify.
why: Even a clear 'why the circle method cannot work here' is useful; but there might be a variant (e.g. Kloosterman refinement, delta method of Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec) that handles equations like ff′ − D = 1 with congruences — these are 'shifted convolution' sums, which DFI's delta method handles with few variables!
first_step: Write the Type II count as a shifted convolution Σ_{ff′ = 4c²dp + 1} with congruences, and check the delta-method literature (DFI 1993; Heath-Brown's version) for the needed uniformity in p.
refs: Heath-Brown, 'A new form of the circle method' (1996)

title: Artin's primitive-root conjecture (Hooley, GRH) as the model for 'a fixed p with a property across infinitely many moduli'
connection: Hooley proves (on GRH) that a fixed a is a primitive root mod infinitely many primes q — a statement about ONE integer a across a family of moduli, via Chebotarev in Kummer fields ℚ(ζ_k, a^{1/k}) + GRH error control. ES: one prime p must have 'a good residue' (a certificate) mod some 4cd, across the family — same shape ('fixed base, varying modulus')! Hooley's method is pointwise in a.
why: This is the closest known shape to ES among proved (conditional) theorems: fixed element, varying field family, existence (indeed density) of good moduli — and it is PROVED (GRH). The repo's survey may have missed it. The key: Artin needs infinitely many good q and gets density; ES needs ONE good (c,d), which is weaker.
first_step: Formulate ES Type I at d = 1 as: 'the ideal factors of (p + 2ci) hit the ray class −p mod 4c for some c' and compare to Hooley's setup (p + 2ci plays the role of a? the field ℚ(i, ζ_{4c})?). Then check whether Hooley's GRH-conditional machinery (effective Chebotarev in ℚ(ζ_k, ·)) gives: for a positive proportion of c ≤ X, the certificate exists — i.e. f(p) → ∞ on GRH?! Check against FRONTIER §5 (conditional results) for what's known on GRH.

refs: C. Hooley, On Artin's conjecture, J. reine angew. Math. 225 (1967) 209–220 (http://eudml.org/doc/150785)

title: Dickson/Schinzel-H-conditional infinite families inside square classes: p such that (4p+1)/5 is a prime ≡ 3 mod 4
connection: If q = (4p+1)/5 is prime with q ≡ 3 mod 4 then 4p+1 = 5q has the divisor q ≡ −1 mod 4 (C = 1) — wait, need a ≡ −1 mod 4C = 4: q ≡ 3 mod 4 ✓. So all such p have C-form certificates. Hypothesis H gives infinitely many primes p with (4p+1)/5 prime in any admissible class; restricted to p in a square class mod 840 (admissible? 4p+1 ≡ 5 mod 3360... need 5 | 4p+1 ⟺ p ≡ 1 mod 5 ✓ compatible with p ≡ 1 mod 840 since 840 = 5·168, p ≡ 1 mod 5 ✓). So: CONDITIONAL on Hypothesis H, there are infinitely many primes in each square class mod 840 satisfying ES via C = 1. Unconditionally: Chen-type sieve gives p with (4p+1)/5 = P₂ (almost prime), not enough (need a factor ≡ 3 mod 4, which a P₂ with both factors ≡ 1 mod 4 lacks).
why: A clean statement of 'conditional infinite families in square classes'; the campaign says no infinite case of ES is proved among hard primes; this item pins the exact unconditional gap: 'infinitely many primes p ≡ 1 mod 840 such that 4p+1 has a prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4' — THIS is a sieve problem (a prime p with 4p+1 having a factor in a residue class) that might be unconditionally provable via sieve + Bombieri–Vinogradov! Check: the set {p : 4p+1 has NO prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4} has density → 0 (like sums of two squares, ~ c/√log x); so infinitely many p ≡ 1 mod 840 with a factor ≡ 3 mod 4 follows from a *lower bound* on primes in the class minus an upper bound on the exceptional subset — the upper bound of Landau type for 4p+1 with p prime needs a sieve (the 'shifted primes with all factors ≡ 1 mod 4' count is ≪ x/(log x)^{3/2} by half-dimensional sieve — PROVABLE).
first_step: Prove: #{p ≤ x, p ≡ 1 (840) : all prime factors of 4p+1 are ≡ 1 mod 4} ≪ x/(log x)^{3/2} via the half-dimensional sieve (Iwaniec) — then since π(x; 840, 1) ≍ x/log x, infinitely many (indeed almost all!) primes p ≡ 1 mod 840 have a C=1 certificate. Check whether the repo already states 'almost all primes in square classes are certified by C = 1' (it surely knows almost-all results, but maybe not this elementary route).

title: Upgrade: 'almost all primes in each square class have a C ≤ K certificate' via a K-fold half-dimensional sieve, with an explicit exponent 3/2 → (1 + K/2)?
connection: Each C adds a condition '4Cp+1 has all factors in a −1-free subgroup H_C'; for C = 1, 2 the subgroup has index 2 (density ~ 1/√log each); the joint exceptional set for C ≤ K has density ~ (log x)^{−K/2} heuristically — a K-dimensional... rather, a sieve of dimension K/2. So #{p ≤ x: no certificate with C ≤ K} ≪ x/(log x)^{1 + K/2} (sieve upper bound, provable for fixed K?). Taking K = K(x) → ∞ slowly gives a Vaughan-type bound by elementary sieve means if uniformity in K holds.
why: Reproduces exceptional-set bounds from the C-form alone and makes the exponent explicit in K — a cleaner path than Vaughan's and a testbed for 'how uniform in K can sieves be' (the Vaughan exp(−c(log)^{2/3}) presumably comes from optimising K vs sieve error).
first_step: Set up the sieve: for fixed K, the condition 'for all C ≤ K, 4Cp+1 ∈ N_{H_C}' is a product of K multiplicative conditions on K linear forms in p; apply the Selberg upper bound sieve with dimension κ = Σ_C (index-related density) and get x/(log x)^{1+κ}; then let K grow; compare with Vaughan.

title: Analogy: Erdős–Odlyzko 'almost all odd n are p + 2^k'-type results vs Romanov — density results for polylog-reservoir problems via second moment; the 'Romanov constant' for ES
connection: Romanov: a positive density of odd n are p + 2^k (reservoir log N). ES's reservoir (certificates) is also polylog and ES's 'Romanov theorem' is the almost-all result (density 1, even). The Romanov method's key is a bound on Σ 1/(ord_q 2) — an arithmetic input about the multiplicative orders. What is the ES analogue of 'Σ 1/ord_q(2) < ∞'? Possibly Σ_C 1/φ(4C)·(…) — the convergence/divergence governs whether density 1 or merely positive density follows.
why: Puts ES's almost-all results in the Romanov–Erdős framework; the analogue of the 'Romanov constant' might be computable and relate to the log²p main term's constant.
first_step: Write the second-moment computation for the C-form à la Romanov; identify the arithmetic sum controlling the variance; compute it.

title: Minimal 'dimension' of ES: is there a one-parameter family of certificates (any type) covering all primes ≤ 10⁷?
connection: The C-form (Type II, c=1) fails for some primes; Type I with c=1 may fail for others; their union might cover everything — or might not, implying that ES is intrinsically 'two-parameter' (any one-parameter sub-family has exceptions). That would be a quantitative version of 'no covering by identities': even infinite one-parameter families don't suffice. [Quick data: below 20000, C-form (Type II, c=1) exceptions are {409, 577, 5569, 9601}; Type I c=1 (f | p²+4d, f ≡ −p mod 4d, d < 1500) has the single exception 2521 ≡ 1 (mod 840); the two sets are disjoint, so the UNION of the two one-parameter forms covers all primes ≡ 1 mod 4 below 20000.]
why: A sharp structural fact about ES, cheap to establish empirically, with implications for proof design (must handle two-parameter families → double sums → the extra log).
first_step: Compute exceptional sets of: C-form; c=1 Type I; e-slice with e ≤ bound (one parameter: e); and their union, for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Sieve for 'poor' failures: #{C ≤ X : ω(4Cp+1) ≤ 5} ≪ X (log log X)⁵/log X — pointwise in p by an upper-bound sieve (Hardy–Ramanujan / Brun) — so most C have rich 4Cp+1
connection: Upper-bound sieves bound the number of C ≤ X for which the linear form 4Cp+1 has few prime factors (almost-prime values of a linear polynomial): ≪ X/log X · (log log X)^k uniformly in p ≤ X^A? (Need uniformity in the coefficient 4p: standard sieve bounds for almost-primes in APs are uniform via Brun–Titchmarsh-type results, with p up to X^{1−ε}... For X = polylog(p) the uniformity fails — the coefficient 4p is huge relative to X. Hmm: the sieve dimension is 1, the sifting range is primes ≤ z; for values 4Cp+1 ≤ 4Xp, we sieve by primes up to z ≈ X^{1/2}: the count of C ≤ X with 4Cp+1 free of primes ≤ z is ≪ X/log z — that's fine and uniform in p (only the residue of p mod q matters). So #{C ≤ X: 4Cp+1 has no prime factor ≤ X^{1/2}} ≪ X/log X — pointwise in p! But 'rich' needs ≥ 6 factors, not just one small factor.) Refine: with k-fold sieving (Erdős–Kac-type for linear forms, Halberstam) one gets most C have ω(4Cp+1) ≈ log log(Xp)… uniformity in p needs the Turán–Kubilius inequality for linear forms with large coefficient — it holds! (The variance Σ_C (ω(4Cp+1) − log log)² ≪ X log log, uniformly in p, since it only uses residues of p mod small primes.)
why: A genuinely pointwise-in-p statement: for any fixed p and X ≥ (log p)^A, almost all C ≤ X have ω(4Cp+1) ≥ 6 (indeed ≈ log log Xp). So 'poor' failures are a vanishing fraction of C. Combined with the Kneser dichotomy, ES(p) would follow if 'periodic rich failures' could be shown not to happen for ALL C — a cleaner target (Galois-type: 'for some C, the prime factors of 4Cp+1 generate a subgroup containing −1 AND the subset-product set is not periodic-avoiding').
first_step: Prove the Turán–Kubilius bound for ω(4Cp+1), C ≤ X, uniform in p (standard; write it out with explicit constants); then count 'rich failures' empirically for p ≤ 10⁵ to see whether they are rare.
refs: Halberstam, 'On the distribution of additive number-theoretic functions' (1955)

title: Ellenberg–Michel–Venkatesh: Linnik's ergodic method with a split-prime condition
connection: EMV prove equidistribution of integer points on spheres (and representations of lattices) assuming a fixed prime splits — Linnik's condition; ES-related ternary representations have exactly this kind of auxiliary prime condition.

connection: If ES(p) held whenever p splits in a fixed field K, Chebotarev would give density; ES needs every p, so need a family of fields covering all splitting types.

connection: If R(p) = trace of Frobenius on some motive (minus main term), Weil bounds give pointwise control ↔ but R(p) is integral-point count, not F_p count.

connection: Maynard's sieve finds bounded gaps between primes in admissible tuples ↔ admissible tuples of p-tied linear forms (4Cp+1 for several C) being simultaneously prime would be ES-hostile (no small divisors).

title: Vinogradov's least-QNR conjecture and ES: n₂(p) ≪ p^ε ⟹ anything?
connection: If ES(p) followed from (q/p) = −1 for every prime q (all forcing lines), then n₂(p) finite would give ES — but forcing lines are open from q = 11.

connection: Iwaniec proved j(m) ≪ (log m)² via sieve ↔ the evasion of certificate classes is a sieve with moduli 4uC−1; can a Jacobsthal-type upper bound show 'every p has a certificate with u ≤ (log p)^2'? No — p is fixed, not a free interval… but the trial variable u is an interval!
why: At fixed p, the variable u ranges over an interval [1, U]; ES Type II with fixed C... the conditions on u are 'u ≡ −p mod (4uC−1)' — modulus depends on u (tied), so not a Jacobsthal sieve. However I3 with t fixed: tuv − u − v = p ⟺ (tu−1)(tv−1) = tp + 1 — a divisor problem of tp+1 for each t. Record the precise mismatch.

connection: #{d | N : d ≡ −1 (mod m)} = φ(m)⁻¹ Σ_{χ mod m} χ(−1) ∏_{q^e‖N} Σ_{j≤e} χ(q)^j. Level failure is the vanishing of this non-negative sum, an identity in the characters' values at N's prime factors.
